exhibits.title: Spoked Wheels
exhibits.change: Light, spoked wheels pulled by horses: speed on land.
exhibits.context: Graves of the Sintashta culture contain the earliest known chariots with spoked wheels. Within a few centuries chariots were used from Egypt to China, reshaping warfare and elite display.
exhibits.significance: A lightweight wheel design that later carried carts, coaches and bicycles.

sources.note: Anthony 2007, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language.

exhibits.title: The Alphabet

when.display: c. 1900–1700 BCE (earliest inscriptions); Phoenician script c. 1050 BCE

regions.note: Phoenician alphabet, ancestor of Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

exhibits.change: A few dozen signs, one per sound — writing anyone could learn.
exhibits.context: Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai adapted hieroglyphs into signs for consonants (the 'ox-head' became aleph, later alpha and A). The Phoenicians spread a standard version around the Mediterranean; Greeks added vowels around 800 BCE.
exhibits.significance: Literacy no longer required mastering hundreds of signs. Most scripts used today descend from this invention.

uncertainty.note: Dating of the earliest inscriptions and the precise route of development are debated.

exhibits.title: Babylonian Mathematics
exhibits.change: Clay tablets solving quadratic problems and approximating √2 to six decimal places.
exhibits.context: Old Babylonian school tablets such as Plimpton 322 (a table related to right triangles) and YBC 7289 (√2 ≈ 1.414213) show a sophisticated mathematical culture built on base-60 place value.
exhibits.significance: Methods for areas, volumes, interest and astronomy that fed into Greek and later mathematics.

uncertainty.note: The purpose of Plimpton 322 is debated.

exhibits.title: The Code of Hammurabi
exhibits.change: 282 laws carved on a basalt stele for all to see.
exhibits.context: The best-known Mesopotamian law code covers trade, property, family, labour and injury, with penalties that often depended on social rank. The stele was later carried to Susa, where it was found in 1901.
exhibits.significance: A landmark of written, public law — and of how law encoded social hierarchy.

exhibits.title: Poverty Point
exhibits.change: Vast concentric earthworks built by hunter-fisher-gatherers.
exhibits.context: Six C-shaped ridges and large mounds were built with millions of basketloads of soil. Materials such as copper and stone arrived from hundreds of kilometres away.
exhibits.significance: Monumental construction and long-distance exchange without farming or states.

exhibits.title: Records of the Sky

when.display: Venus records c. 17th century BCE; daily astronomical diaries from 652 BCE

exhibits.change: Systematic observations, kept for centuries, made the sky predictable.
exhibits.context: The Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa preserves observations from the Old Babylonian period. From 652 BCE scribes kept nightly astronomical diaries; by the later first millennium BCE they predicted lunar and planetary phenomena with arithmetic schemes.
exhibits.significance: The longest continuous scientific record of the ancient world — a foundation for Greek astronomy.

exhibits.title: A Surgical Textbook

when.display: c. 1600 BCE (copy of an older text)

exhibits.change: Forty-eight injury cases, each with examination, diagnosis and treatment.
exhibits.context: The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes wounds, fractures and dislocations in a systematic, largely practical way, including the first known description of the brain's surface. The Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) collects hundreds of remedies.
exhibits.significance: An early example of case-based, observational medicine.

exhibits.title: Shang Bronze Casting
exhibits.change: Ritual vessels cast in multi-piece clay moulds, some weighing hundreds of kilograms.
exhibits.context: Chinese bronze-workers developed piece-mould casting rather than the lost-wax method common in the west, producing highly standardised, intricately decorated vessels in large workshops.
exhibits.significance: Industrial-scale organised production in the Bronze Age.

exhibits.title: The Rhind Papyrus

when.display: c. 1550 BCE (copied from a text c. 200 years older)

exhibits.change: Eighty-four worked problems: fractions, areas, volumes, rations.
exhibits.context: Copied by the scribe Ahmose, the papyrus teaches Egyptian arithmetic with unit fractions and approximates the area of a circle.
exhibits.significance: A window into practical mathematics used to run a state.

exhibits.title: The Olmec

site.label: San Lorenzo and La Venta, Gulf Coast

exhibits.change: Mesoamerica's first great centres, with colossal carved heads.
exhibits.context: Olmec centres at San Lorenzo and La Venta built earthen platforms, moved multi-tonne basalt monuments and traded jade and obsidian widely. Many later Mesoamerican traditions — the ballgame, calendars, perhaps writing — have Olmec roots.
exhibits.significance: The foundations of an independent civilisational tradition in the Americas.

uncertainty.note: Whether the Olmec were a 'mother culture' or one of several interacting cultures is debated.

exhibits.title: Lapita Voyagers

regions.note: Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa.

exhibits.change: Outrigger canoes carried families, crops and animals into the open Pacific.
exhibits.context: Makers of distinctive dentate-stamped Lapita pottery sailed from the Bismarck Archipelago as far as Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries, crossing gaps of hundreds of kilometres to islands never before inhabited.
exhibits.significance: The first settlement of Remote Oceania — the start of the greatest maritime expansion before modern times.

exhibits.title: The Uluburun Shipwreck
exhibits.change: One ship's cargo drew on at least seven cultures.
exhibits.context: The wreck carried ten tonnes of copper and one of tin ingots, glass ingots, ebony, ivory, amber from the Baltic, and goods from Egypt, Canaan, Cyprus and the Aegean.
exhibits.significance: A snapshot of a deeply interconnected Late Bronze Age Mediterranean.

exhibits.title: Oracle-Bone Script
exhibits.change: Questions to the ancestors, carved into bone — the oldest Chinese writing.
exhibits.context: Late Shang diviners inscribed ox scapulae and turtle shells with questions and answers about harvests, war and illness. The script is the direct ancestor of Chinese characters used today.
exhibits.significance: An independent invention of writing, continuously used for over 3,000 years.

exhibits.title: Iron

regions.note: Independent invention in sub-Saharan Africa is argued but debated.

exhibits.change: An abundant ore became the everyday metal of tools and weapons.
exhibits.context: Iron objects were rare and precious for centuries; after about 1200 BCE bloomery smelting and forging spread across the eastern Mediterranean and beyond. Unlike copper and tin, iron ore is found almost everywhere.
exhibits.significance: Cheap, common metal put tools in the hands of ordinary farmers and soldiers.

uncertainty.note: Where iron smelting began, and whether it was independently invented in Africa, are debated.
